reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Results from failure of normal segmentation of the cervical vertebrae, producing congenital fusion of two or more cervical segments
The classic clinical triad is a short neck, a low posterior hairline, and restricted neck movement, though not all features are present in every case
Fusion may be limited to a single level or extensive, and the clinical severity varies accordingly
Associated anomalies are common and include scoliosis, Sprengel deformity, hearing loss, and cardiac and renal malformations
Neurological risk arises because fused segments concentrate stress on adjacent mobile levels, predisposing to instability and cord injury
It may occur in isolation or as part of broader spectrums such as the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum
Wildervanck syndrome is a related presentation adding sensorineural deafness and Duane retraction anomaly, seen chiefly in females
reference.pathophysiology: Klippel-Feil syndrome originates from a disturbance of somite segmentation and resegmentation in the cervical region during early embryogenesis, so that adjacent vertebrae fail to separate and instead fuse. This defective segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm produces the shortened, immobile cervical spine and low hairline, and the same developmental window overlaps with the formation of the ear, heart, kidneys, and scapula, accounting for the associated anomalies. Some familial forms are linked to variants in genes governing segmentation and mesodermal patterning, while many cases are sporadic. The fused rigid segments alter cervical biomechanics, transferring load to neighbouring mobile levels and creating a long-term risk of degenerative change and instability.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired cervical fusion from juvenile arthritis
additionalInvestigations: Cervical spine radiographs including flexion-extension views to detect fusion and instability
Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine to assess the cord and craniocervical junction
Echocardiography to screen for congenital heart disease
Renal ultrasound to detect urinary tract anomalies
Assessment for scoliosis and Sprengel deformity
redFlags: Neurological signs suggesting cervical cord compression or myelopathy
Craniocervical or segmental instability increasing the risk of catastrophic cord injury
New or progressive weakness, numbness, or sphincter disturbance
High anaesthetic risk from restricted neck movement and potential instability
Significant undiagnosed cardiac or renal malformation
reference.prognosis: Many individuals with limited fusion lead normal lives, but extensive fusion or associated instability carries a lifelong risk of neurological injury and degenerative disease, and activities with high cervical impact are generally discouraged.
pitfalls: Overlooking cervical instability and clearing patients for contact sport or manipulation
Failing to anticipate a difficult airway from restricted neck extension
Missing associated hearing, cardiac, and renal anomalies
Not recognising Wildervanck syndrome when deafness and Duane anomaly coexist
Attributing new neurological symptoms to unrelated causes rather than adjacent-level stress
